statement: A major strand of scholarship reconstructs a historical convergence in which Yahweh came to absorb or be identified with El's titles, functions, and senior position within Israelite religion; this is a merger/assimilation model, not a claim that Yahweh and El were always identical.

sources.citation: Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford University Press, 2001), ch. 7, “El, Yahweh, and the Original God of Israel and the Exodus.”
sources.author: Mark S. Smith
sources.access_note: Oxford contents and chapter metadata explicitly frame El/Yahweh and the original god of Israel as a historical problem.

sources.citation: Theodore J. Lewis, The Origin and Character of God (Oxford University Press, 2020), ch. 4, “El Worship,” and ch. 6, “The Origin of Yahweh.”
sources.author: Theodore J. Lewis
sources.access_note: Lewis separately treats El worship and Yahweh's historical origin, allowing convergence to be modeled without collapsing the two origin questions.

sources.citation: John Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan (Sheffield Academic Press, 2000), ch. 1, “Yahweh and El.”
sources.author: John Day
sources.access_note: Book contents identify Yahweh-and-El as a dedicated historical-comparative chapter.

does_not_demonstrate: This does not demonstrate that Yahweh and El were always the same deity.
This does not settle Yahweh's geographic origin; a southern-origin model can coexist with later El/Yahweh convergence.
This does not make every Hebrew use of 'el' a reference to the Canaanite proper-name deity.
adversarial_counter: Yahweh's earliest origin may lie outside the Canaanite pantheon, making the historically reconstructed El/Yahweh relationship a later assimilation rather than original identity.
